name: Iris Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a site foreperson for a small contractor that refurbishes council flats, mostly the Ashdown blocks on the north side of town. We go in while people are still living there and put in new windows, doors, kitchens and insulation, so half my job is carpentry and half is keeping Mrs Okafor in flat 12 from crying because her kitchen's in her hallway. I love the before and after, when an old lady can finally keep her flat warm. What wears me out is doing a team leader's job on a carpenter's wage, and the paperwork that comes with it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's on your team, and what does home look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've got six on the crew, two joiners, a plasterer called Rosa who I eat lunch with on the stairwell, and three general hands. At home it's Joel, he drives a delivery van, and our two, Maya who's fourteen and Sam who's ten. We've got a mortgage on a terrace off Canal Street and, honestly, about three weeks of money if everything stopped.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned paperwork. Do you use any AI for it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. Maya showed me how to paste my scribbled snag list into a chatbot and get a tidy report back, and it saves me an evening a week. I check every line, though, because it once told the office a window was fitted when I'd written that it wasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I expected, it's a clever notepad and that's all. At work I'd joke that the robot still can't calm down a tenant. Online I probably wouldn't bother saying anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my problems stay the problems they are now. The council keeps squeezing the contract price, and that comes out of our wages and our timelines, not out of AI. I'd still be three weeks from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing, and keep using the chatbot for the snag lists because it saves me Tuesday evenings. I'd keep pushing in the union for the council contracts to set a proper pay rate. Nothing new, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the tech. Tired about the money, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the council squeezes the contract price. What does that look like on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like eight days to refit a flat that needs ten, so we rush the last two. The cheapest bid wins, and the cheapest bid is always paid for by somebody's knees. Usually Rosa's, or mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what would you most like to change anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like the pay to match the job. I sign off on the work, I deal with the tenants and the council inspector, and I'm paid like a joiner. Even an extra hundred a month would mean we could save something.

S0.say: I'd say AI turned out to be a clever notepad, about what I expected. At work I'd joke that the robot still can't calm down an upset tenant.
S0.think: I think my real problems would stay the same: council contracts squeezing prices, wages and timelines. I'd still be about three weeks of savings from trouble.
S0.do: Keeps working as foreperson and keeps using the chatbot to write up snag lists. Pushes through the union for council contracts to set a fair pay rate.
S0.feel: Calm about the technology, tired about the money.
S0.quote: The cheapest bid wins, and the cheapest bid is always paid for by somebody's knees.
S0.fieldNote: Iris has already found a small, practical use for AI and treats it like any other tool, checking its mistakes. Her pressure comes from low-bid council contracts rather than technology. She frames everything through the tenants and her crew's bodies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it needs to be done properly, with training paid for by the firms and the council, not dumped on workers. At work I'd tell the crew we'll learn whatever comes, together. I'd probably share the union's statement online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the paperwork side of my job goes first, and that's fine. But if the office can schedule everything with AI, they might decide they don't need a foreperson, just a joiner with a tablet. And I'm the expensive one, even though I'm cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until I saw what actually landed on our sites, I'm not buying anything on a rumour. Once the other crews started using a tool that worked, I'd learn it properly, probably on a Saturday course if the union got it funded. I'd use the chatbot more for the planning side so I'm the one who knows it best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared yet, more like watching weather come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the expensive one even though you're cheap. What did you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm paid less than most forepersons in the region, but I'm still the highest wage on my crew. So when they look for savings, they start with the one person who knows where all the bodies are buried. Not real bodies, I mean the dodgy wiring behind the plasterboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rosa if her side of the work started shrinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to come with me to whatever course is on. Rosa's brilliant but she hates screens, she still writes her hours on the back of her hand. I'd sit with her and do it, the same way Maya sat with me.

S1.say: I'd say change needs to be done properly, with training paid for by firms and the council rather than dumped on workers. I'd tell my crew we'd learn whatever comes together.
S1.think: I think the paperwork goes first, which is fine, but the office might then decide it doesn't need a foreperson. As the highest wage on the crew, I'd be the obvious saving.
S1.do: Waits to see which tools actually reach the sites before acting. Learns the proven ones on a union-funded Saturday course and uses the chatbot more for planning.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like watching bad weather come in.
S1.quote: So when they look for savings, they start with the one person who knows where all the bodies are buried.
S1.fieldNote: Iris's worry is specific: her role as the link between office and site could be squeezed. She wants proof before she acts, then plans to learn properly and bring her crew along. She thinks about the people around her, like Rosa, as much as herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this should never have been allowed to happen this fast, and that whoever owns these machines should pay for the people they replace. I'd be on every union call. I'd say it out loud at the school gate too, because every parent there is in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd lose the house. Joel's van job would go just as fast as mine, delivery is the obvious one for robots. Two wages gone in two years with three weeks of savings, that's not a plan, that's a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd cancel everything we don't need: the streaming, Sam's swimming, the holiday deposit we haven't paid yet. I'd go to the union and the council's housing office early, before we're behind, not after. I'd ask my mum if we could move in with her if it came to it, and I'd hate asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Properly. I'd be up at three in the morning doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only act once things are proven. In two years, is there time to wait for proof?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's the bit that gets me. My whole way of doing things is watch first, then move. With two years, by the time I've seen it work on someone else's site, it's already on mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Maya and Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maya would want the truth, she's fourteen and she reads everything. I'd tell her we might have to move to Nana's and that it's not her fault or ours. Sam I'd just tell we're having an adventure, and he'd see through it in a week.

S2.say: I'd say this should never have been allowed to happen so fast, and owners of the machines should pay for the people they replace. I'd say it on union calls and at the school gate.
S2.think: I think we'd lose the house, because Joel's delivery job would go as fast as mine. Two wages gone in two years with three weeks of savings is a countdown.
S2.do: Cancels streaming, swimming lessons and the holiday plans in the first month. Goes to the union and the council housing office early and asks her mother about moving in if needed.
S2.feel: Frightened, awake at three in the morning doing sums.
S2.quote: With two years, by the time I've seen it work on someone else's site, it's already on mine.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture breaks Iris's usual method of waiting for proof, and she names that herself. Both household incomes are exposed, which makes this far worse than her own job alone. She blames owners of the machines and leans on the union, council and family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for the council and the unions to set up proper retraining, and I'd be pushing for it hard. I'd say it at work and I'd sign every petition going. I'd tell people to learn the new kit before it's forced on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to watch it arrive on other sites first, which is how I like to do things. It's not enough to save much, but it's enough to get Joel into something less exposed. I'd want us to switch roles so one of us has a safer income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year of seeing it coming, I'd put whatever I could aside, even forty a month, and talk to Joel about him training for something like care work or maintenance. By year two or three I'd be on whatever course teaches people to oversee the robots on a refurb site. When it arrives I'd want to be the one who checks their work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. It's the difference between being chased and being late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks the robot's work, in your mind? What does that job look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone who knows what a bad fit looks like. A robot can hang a door, but it won't notice the floor's sloped because the old joists are rotten underneath. Somebody has to know what an old building is hiding, and that's twenty years of knees on floorboards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want Joel to change first. What would that conversation be like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the washing up, probably, that's where we have the big ones. He'd say why him and not me, and I'd say because I've got the better chance of a role checking robots. He'd say fair enough after a day of sulking.

S3.say: I'd say five years gives councils and unions time to set up proper retraining, and I'd push hard for it. I'd tell people to learn new kit before it's forced on them.
S3.think: I think five years lets me watch it arrive elsewhere first, which suits me. It's not enough to save much, but it's enough to move my partner into a safer job.
S3.do: Saves around forty a month and talks Joel into training for care or maintenance work. Takes a course in overseeing robots on refurbishment sites within two or three years.
S3.feel: Anxious but with a plan, more like running late than being chased.
S3.quote: Somebody has to know what an old building is hiding, and that's twenty years of knees on floorboards.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits Iris's watch-then-move style, and her mood drops a notch accordingly. Her plan is a household plan: spread the risk between two earners. She believes old buildings need human judgement, which gives her a clear idea of where she still fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right, so let's not waste it like we wasted ten years on insulation. I'd say that at work and at union meetings. I'd want the council to start the training now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the most hopeful one for me. I'd be fifty-three, Maya would be through college and Sam nearly there. It still ends the same, but I'd have time to move into something safer, maybe inspecting work for the council instead of doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first couple of years watching which jobs actually survive, then train for the strongest one, probably building inspection. I'd save, slowly, and I'd make sure Maya picks a college course that won't be gone by the time she finishes. I'd vote for whoever puts real money into retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's an uneasy I can carry. I'd be sad for the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you mean about wasting ten years on insulation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone knew for years these flats were losing heat through the walls. Nobody paid to fix it until bills went through the roof, and then it was all rush jobs. We always see it coming and we always pay for it late, so ten years only helps if somebody starts on day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Maya's course. What is she thinking of now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to do graphic design, which would have been my first pick to worry about with AI. I'd sit her down and look at it together, not tell her no. If she still wants it after we've looked, fine, it's her life.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so it shouldn't be wasted the way years were wasted on insulating flats. I'd want the council to start training now.
S4.think: I think ten years is the most hopeful picture for me, at fifty-three with my children nearly grown. I could move into safer work, perhaps inspecting rather than doing.
S4.do: Watches which jobs survive for a couple of years, then trains for the strongest, probably building inspection. Saves slowly, reviews her daughter's college choice with her, and votes for parties funding retraining.
S4.feel: Uneasy but manageable, with sadness for the trade.
S4.quote: We always see it coming and we always pay for it late, so ten years only helps if somebody starts on day one.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Iris sounds almost practical about it, mapping a move to inspection. Her lesson from council insulation work shapes her view that time only helps if someone acts early. She doesn't impose her fears on her daughter, which fits her steady, wait-and-check style.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits Joel and me at once and doesn't give me time to see what works. What would help is help with the mortgage while we retrain, and training that's free and on weekends, not something you have to give up a wage to do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about the tenants. Everyone's asking what happens to builders, but nobody's asking who Mrs Okafor phones when the robot leaves a draught.

headlineQuote: Everyone's asking what happens to builders, but nobody's asking who Mrs Okafor phones when the robot leaves a draught.
portrait: Iris Abbott is a 43-year-old foreperson refitting council flats, with two kids, a partner who drives a delivery van, a mortgage and about three weeks of savings. She uses a chatbot now and then for paperwork and checks every line it writes. She's union-minded and likes to see a change proven before she moves. She is calm about the plateau and uneasy about steady disruption, then alarmed by AGI in two years because both household incomes would go before she could watch and learn. With five or ten years she builds a family plan around retraining Joel and moving herself towards checking or inspecting work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would take both her job and her partner's and give her no time to see what works first.
whatWouldHelp: Mortgage help while they retrain, and free weekend training that doesn't mean giving up a wage.
